section: 4. Quality checks and comparison with 2023 features
text:
4. Quality checks and comparison with 2023 features
Compare equivalent 2023 outputs with the earlier well-crop feature table using its original location and rounding conventions. Do not interpret unmatched areas as zero land use.


Code
def compare_gavin(repo, crops_root):
    observations = pd.read_csv(paths.NITRATE_CLEAN,
                               dtype={"gm_well_id": "string"},
                               parse_dates=["gm_samp_collection_date"])
    wells_2024 = observations[observations.gm_samp_collection_date.dt.year.eq(2024)].gm_well_id.unique()
    expected = pd.read_csv(repo / "notebooks/data_cleaning/crop_mapping/well_crop_features_all.csv",
                           dtype={"well_id": "string"})
    legacy_wells = pd.read_csv(repo / "notebooks/data_cleaning/crop_mapping/wells_nitrate.csv",
                               dtype={"well_id": "string"})
    ids = set(wells_2024) & set(expected.well_id) & set(legacy_wells.well_id)
    legacy_wells = legacy_wells[legacy_wells.well_id.isin(ids)].copy()
    points = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
        legacy_wells[["well_id", "x_m", "y_m"]].rename(columns={"well_id": "gm_well_id"}),
        geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(legacy_wells.x_m, legacy_wells.y_m), crs=METRIC_CRS)
    path = find_gdb(crops_root, "2023")
    info = pyogrio.read_info(path, layer=pyogrio.list_layers(path)[0, 0])
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = points.total_bounds
    bbox = Transformer.from_crs(METRIC_CRS, info["crs"], always_xy=True).transform_bounds(
        xmin - 1001, ymin - 1001, xmax + 1001, ymax + 1001, densify_pts=41)
    layer = pyogrio.list_layers(path)[0, 0]
    map_data = pyogrio.read_dataframe(path, layer=layer, bbox=bbox)
    map_data.geometry = map_data.geometry.force_2d().to_crs(METRIC_CRS).buffer(0)
    map_data = map_data[map_data.COUNTY.eq("Monterey")].copy()
    letters = map_data.SYMB_CLASS.astype("string").str.split("|").str[0].str.strip().str.upper()
    map_data["crop_group"] = letters.map(CLASS_GROUP)
    map_data.loc[letters.str.startswith("U", na=False), "crop_group"] = "urban"
    map_data["crop_cycles"] = map_data.MULTIUSE.astype("string").str.strip().map(CYCLES).fillna(1)
    map_data = map_data[map_data.crop_group.notna()]
    legacy = expected.set_index("well_id")
    output = []
    for radius in RADII:
        table, _ = summarize(points, map_data, radius)
        for well_id, row in table.iterrows():
            for col, value in row.items():
                if not (col.startswith("pct_") and "_of_mapped_" not in col) and not col.startswith("crop_cycles_"):
                    continue
                feature = col.replace(f"_{radius}m", f"_{radius}m_2023")
                old = legacy.loc[well_id, feature]
                # Gavin rounded saved features to 3 decimals; these locations and
                # his Monterey filter reproduce those legacy calculation inputs.
                match = (pd.isna(value) and pd.isna(old)) or np.isclose(
                    value, old, atol=0.000501, rtol=0)
                output.append({"well_id": well_id, "feature": feature,
                               "recomputed_at_gavin_coordinates": value,
                               "gavin_saved_rounded_3dp": old,
                               "absolute_difference": abs(value - old) if pd.notna(value) and pd.notna(old) else np.nan,
                               "matches_rounding_tolerance": bool(match)})
    result = pd.DataFrame(output)
    require(result.matches_rounding_tolerance.all(), "Gavin 2023 validation failed.")
    return result

from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay, PrecisionRecallDisplay, RocCurveDisplay, confusion_matrix, average_precision_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, balanced_accuracy_score, brier_score_loss

CONFIG = ("10km_subbasin", True)      # which configuration to plot
THRESHOLDS = [0.25, 0.3, 0.35, 0.4, 0.45, 0.5]         # probabilities at or above which a sample is called an exceedance
DARKEST, LIGHTEST = 0.0, 0.6          # 0 = black, 1 = white; 0.6 is a medium gray
n = len(THRESHOLDS)
THRESHOLD_COLORS = {t: str(DARKEST + (LIGHTEST - DARKEST) * i / (n - 1)) for i, t in enumerate(THRESHOLDS)}
MARKERS = ["D", "v", "P", "o", "s", "^", "X", "*"]
THRESHOLD_MARKERS = {t: MARKERS[i] for i, t in enumerate(THRESHOLDS)}
FIGURES = paths.FIGURES["classification"]
FIGURES.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

dev = devs[CONFIG]
y_true = dev["exceeds"].to_numpy()
folds = dev["fold"].to_numpy()
prevalence = y_true.mean()

TAG = f"{CONFIG[0]}, subbasin features={CONFIG[1]}"


def panels(n, ncols=3, width=4.5, height=3.8):
    """A grid with one panel per model (or metric); unused panels are hidden."""
    nrows = -(-n // ncols)                            # ceiling division
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width * ncols, height * nrows), squeeze=False)
    axs = axs.ravel()
    for ax in axs[n:]:
        ax.set_axis_off()
    return fig, axs


def save(fig, name):
    fig.savefig(FIGURES / f"{name}_{CONFIG[0]}_subbasin{int(CONFIG[1])}.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")


def threshold_counts(prob, threshold):
    """Confusion-matrix counts and rates when samples with prob >= threshold are called exceedances."""
    predicted = (prob >= threshold).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, predicted, labels=[0, 1]).ravel()
    return {
        "missed_exceedances": fn, 
        "false_alarms": fp,
        "recall": tp / (tp + fn),
        "precision": tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else np.nan,
        "false_positive_rate": fp / (fp + tn),
        "share_flagged": (tp + fp) / len(y_true)
    }

Choosing a model and a threshold
The goal of this project is to identify areas of potentially high nitrate risk for the sake of public health and to minimize the cost of deploying VTS. Thus, we wish to maximize both recall and precision.
Of all the models, the random forest is the most stable across folds and appears to be the strongest performer overall. We choose our final model to be a random forest classifier, with a threshold of 0.4.

title: Predicting Areas of High-Risk Nitrate Pollution in Salinas Valley
text:
Problem Statement
Agricultural runoff carries pollutants into rivers and coastal waters, harming ecosystems and water quality. Vegetated Treatment Systems (VTS), such as bioreactors, constructed wetlands and vegetated ditches, can help reduce this pollution, but they are not equally effective everywhere. Their success depends on where they are placed, how they are designed, and how well they are maintained.
This project will predict areas with higher risk of nitrate pollution in the Salinas Valley, California, and determine where additional monitoring is most needed. We will train our model on nitrate pollutant measurements in groundwater wells throughout the Salinas Valley and use soil characteristics, precipitation, temperature, and types of cropland as predictor variables. Once areas with high nitrate risk have been identified and monitored, this data can be used to propose locations for VTS infrastructure.


Interactive groundwater nitrate risk map



Interactive map of the Salinas Valley, colored by low, moderate, and high risk of nitrate groundwater contamination predictions from our modelling. The layers show the risk assessment from our fitted Random Forest Classifer (Random Forest Model) and a hybrid model using our fitted Random Forest Classifer and the last groundwater measurement in that area (Hybrid Model).




Data sources
This project uses data from several publicly accessible resources:

United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Natural Resources Conversation Service (NRCS) Web Soil Survey/SSURGO: https://websoilsurvey.nrcs.usda.gov/
United States Geological Survey (USGS) National Hydrography: https://www.usgs.gov/national-hydrography
California Natural Resources Agency, California Department of Water Resources crop mapping: https://data.cnra.ca.gov/dataset/statewide-crop-mapping
USDA Cropland Data Layer: https://data.nass.usda.gov/Research_and_Science/Cropland/sarsfaqs2.php
PRISM Climate Group: https://prism.oregonstate.edu/
California Open Data, GAMA - Irrigated Lands Regulatory Program: http://gamagroundwater.waterboards.ca.gov/gama/datadownload



Key performance indicators
The project is concerned with two factors: safety of public health, and cost of deploying and maintaining VTS. Nitrate pollution in water exceeding 10 mg/L is deemed harmful. We prioritize recall. If there is an actual exceedance above 10 mg/L, we need our model to capture it. Precision is a secondary priority. We do not want to deploy VTS in areas where it is not needed.


Data exploration

Groundwater Cleaning
Soil Features
Precipitation Data
Crop Mapping



Data splitting strategy and limitations
We needed to adopt a data splitting strategy that accounts for the fact that nearby wells have similar nitrate levels. We also made sure to divide the percentage of exceedances among each fold. We used the strategy from Ref. [3], dividing our map into a square grid, performing a group k-fold split, and grouping points inside the grid cell. We evaluated the data leakage by comparing the RMSE of a k-nearest-neighbors (kNN) model to a model outputting the training mean. “Estimated leakage” is defined as \(1 - \frac{\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{KNN}}}{\mathrm{RMSE}_\mathrm{mean}}\), where \(\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{KNN}}\) is the root mean squared error of the kNN estimator and \(\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{mean}}\) is the root mean squared error of predicting the mean. If the kNN estimator performs similarly to predicting the mean, then the estimated leakage should be approximately 0; positive values indicate that kNN is performing better. We found that 10 km equal-area cells had approximately no leakage.
However, from preliminary modeling with this data split strategy, we found large variation in scoring across folds, with some folds performing much worse. We realized that grid cells inside the Salinas Valley subbasins were not being uniformly distributed among folds. Altering our data split strategy again, we created a subbasin-stratefied split, finding good fold-to-fold stability, with little leakage, with 5 km and above size subbasin-stratefied splits. In the end, we chose the 10 km subbasin split, since we did not perform extensive leakage testing, and we preferred to be conservative. The resulting limitation of our model is that it cannot easily generalize to new locations, and relies upon stratification amongst subbasin data.






Figure 1: Geographical distribution of the groundwater dataset with the final splitting strategy, stratefied by both subbasin and exceedance.





Modeling plan and results

Feature Selection
Regression
Classification

We approached modeling from two angles: regression and classification. The regression task seeks to directly predict the nitrate pollutant concentration. We compared a dummy model and simple linear model to linear models with two regularization strategies (ridge and lasso), a decision tree model, a random forest model, and an XGBoost regressor. Per model, we tuned hyperparameters with extensive nested cross validation, using GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV in each set of training folds, holding one whole fold out at the time, so the test fold is never used for tuning. Our base scoring metric was RMSE, where our lowest RMSE came from the random forest model, averaging 0.973 per fold, with only small improvement over the dummy, 1.208. Plots of predicted nitrate values versus observed nitrate values showed poor reproductions of real trends, with high residuals. We concluded that the features available did not encode enough information to produce accurate regression models.
The classification task seeks to classify locations as exceedances (above nitrate concentrations of 10 mg/L) or non-exceedances. We compared a dummy model and simple logistic model to logistic models with two regularization strategies (L1 and L2), a decision tree model, a random forest model, and an XGBoost classifier. Our basic scoring metric was AUC score, where again the random forest was the strongest performing, averaging 0.827 across training folds,, compared to the weakest performing, the decision tree model, with an AUC of 0.765. Per our KPIs, the f1 score, balancing recall and precision, was highest for the random forest model with the slightly lower cutoff threshold of ~0.4, with an f1 of 0.673. We found the random forest model to be the most stable across folds and perform the strongest overall.
On our final model evaluation with the holdout set, our random forest classifer performance ended up being weaker, with an AUC of 0.741, compared with 0.827. Similarly, the f1 dips to 0.654 at a cutoff threshold of 0.4. Upon some investigation, we found that this particular fold had a much higher percentage of exceedances (42%, compared to ~30% in the training folds), which suggests weaker extrapolation to the unseen data. Essentially, the model generalizes to unseen areas about as well as cross-validation suggests when every subbasin is represented, but it performs worse where a heavily contaminated subbasin is under-represented in training. In the future, we should be more thorough in our splitting strategy, ensuring that the training and holdout contained more general representations of the dataset.






Figure 2: The ROC AUC curve, precision-recall tradeoff, calibration, and confusion matrix for our fitted Random Forest Classifer on the final holdout set.





Next steps
We see three next steps. First, would like to add additional features that explain why nitrate builds up, like how deep the wells are and how much fertilizer is applied compared to what crops use. We want to test the model again on new 2026 samples from every part of the Salinas Valley.
Second, we plan to explore the possibility of creating a hybrid model that combines our predictions with real measurements. For instance, where a well nearby has been tested, we can use that, but where nobody has tested, the model fills the gap. A hybrid modeling approach points to 318 small areas where nitrate is likely too high and no one has tested the water.
Third, using this hybrid modeling approach, together with new drainage, available space, soils and community needs, we can help choose where to build plant-based systems that clean farm runoff.


Selected scientific references
[1] Ransom et al. (2017), A hybrid machine learning model to predict and visualize nitrate concentration throughout the Central Valley aquifer: https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70187880
[2] Nolan, Fienen & Lorenz (2015), A statistical learning framework for groundwater nitrate models of the Central Valley: https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70157562
[3] Belitz et al., 2010, Estimation of aquifer scale proportion using equal area grids: Assessment of regional scale groundwater quality: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2010WR009321

Code
points = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    depth_clean.copy(),
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(
        depth_clean["longitude"],
        depth_clean["latitude"]
    ),
    crs="EPSG:4326"

projected_crs = "EPSG:32610"

points = points.to_crs(projected_crs)
boundary = huc8.to_crs(projected_crs)

watershed = boundary.geometry.union_all()

# Keep sampling locations within the watershed
points = points.loc[points.geometry.within(watershed)].copy()

# Generate Voronoi polygons
voronoi = voronoi_polygons(
    MultiPoint(points.geometry.tolist()),
    extend_to=watershed.envelope
)

# Convert polygons to a GeoDataFrame
thiessen = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    geometry=list(voronoi.geoms),
    crs=projected_crs
)

# Clip every polygon to the HUC8 boundary
thiessen["geometry"] = thiessen.geometry.intersection(watershed)

# Remove empty geometries
thiessen = thiessen.loc[
    ~thiessen.geometry.is_empty
].copy()


# Find the nearest sampling point to each polygon's representative point
point_geometries = points.geometry

def nearest_point_index(polygon):
    representative_point = polygon.representative_point()
    return point_geometries.distance(representative_point).idxmin()

nearest_indices = thiessen.geometry.apply(nearest_point_index)

attributes = points.drop(columns="geometry")

thiessen = thiessen.join(
    attributes.loc[nearest_indices].reset_index(drop=True)
)

    wells_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(wells[["well_id"]], geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(wells["x_m"], wells["y_m"]), crs=3310)
    print(wells_gdf.head())
    results = []

    for year, (zip_name, code_col, county_col) in files.items():
        print("working on", year)

        zip_path = "crop_maps/" + zip_name
        names = zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path).namelist()
        gdb = [n.split(".gdb")[0] + ".gdb" for n in names if ".gdb" in n]
        shp = [n for n in names if n.endswith(".shp")]
        map_path = "/vsizip/" + zip_path + "/" + (gdb[0] if gdb else shp[0])
        if county_col is None:
            m = gpd.read_file(map_path, engine="pyogrio")
        else:
            m = gpd.read_file(map_path, where=f"{county_col} = 'Monterey'", engine="pyogrio")

        letters = m[code_col].astype(str).str.split("|").str[0].str.strip().str.upper()
        m["group"] = letters.map(letter_to_group).fillna("other")
        m.loc[letters.str.startswith("U"), "group"] = "urban"

        # crops per year is only mapped from 2018 on
        if year >= 2018:
            m["cycles"] = m["MULTIUSE"].map(crops_per_year).fillna(1)
        else:
            m["cycles"] = -1

        m["geometry"] = m.geometry.force_2d()
        m = m.to_crs(3310)
        m["geometry"] = m.geometry.buffer(0)
        m = m.dissolve(by=["group", "cycles"]).reset_index()

        # 500 and 1000 meter radius around the wells
        for radius in ([500, 1000] if year == 2023 else [1000]):
            # cut the crop shapes with a circle around each well, as % of the circle
            circles = wells_gdf.copy()
            circles["geometry"] = wells_gdf.buffer(radius)
            pieces = gpd.overlay(circles, m, how="intersection", keep_geom_type=True)
            pieces["pct"] = pieces.geometry.area / (np.pi * radius ** 2) * 100

            # add up per well and group
            table = pieces.pivot_table(index="well_id", columns="group", values="pct", aggfunc="sum")
            table = table.reindex(index=wells["well_id"], columns=farmed_groups + ["idle_fallow", "urban"]).fillna(0)
            table["cropland"] = table[farmed_groups].sum(axis=1)

            # crops per year (area weighted) and % multi-cropped
            if year >= 2018:
                crop = pieces[pieces["group"].isin(farmed_groups)]
                table["crop_cycles"] = (crop["pct"] * crop["cycles"]).groupby(crop["well_id"]).sum() / crop.groupby("well_id")["pct"].sum()
                table["multicrop"] = crop[crop["cycles"] >= 2].groupby("well_id")["pct"].sum()
                table["multicrop"] = table["multicrop"].fillna(0)

            # names like pct_veg_berry_1000m_2023 and crop_cycles_1000m_2023
            new_names = []
            for col in table.columns:
                if col == "crop_cycles":
                    new_names.append(f"crop_cycles_{radius}m_{year}")
                else:
                    new_names.append(f"pct_{col}_{radius}m_{year}")
            table.columns = new_names
            results.append(table)

    # distance from each well to the nearest vegetable/berry field
    veg_fields = m[m["group"] == "veg_berry"][["geometry"]].explode(index_parts=False)
    nearest = gpd.sjoin_nearest(wells_gdf, veg_fields, distance_col="dist_veg_berry_m_2023")
    results.append(nearest.groupby("well_id")["dist_veg_berry_m_2023"].min())

    features = pd.concat(results, axis=1).round(3)
    features.index.name = "well_id"
    features.reset_index().to_csv(features_file, index=False)

## Globally using interquartile range method. 
## Anything above 75% percentile.
# 
def flag_outliers(df):
    q1 = df["nitrate_mg_L"].quantile(0.25)
    q3 = df["nitrate_mg_L"].quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1

    #print(f"Interquartile range: {iqr:.3f}")
    lower = 0
    upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr

    df = df.copy()
    df["is_outlier"] = (
        (df["nitrate_mg_L"] < lower) |
        (df["nitrate_mg_L"] > upper)
    )
    return df

def temporal_analysis(start_year, end_year, groundwater, groundwater_period):
    groundwater_filtered = groundwater[
        groundwater["gm_samp_collection_date"].dt.year.between(
            start_year, end_year
        )
    ].copy()

    # Count unique time datapoints for each coordinate pair
    temporal_counts = (
        groundwater_filtered
        .groupby(["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude"])["gm_samp_collection_date"]
        .nunique()
        .reset_index(name="num_timepoints")
        .sort_values("num_timepoints")
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )

    mean_count = temporal_counts["num_timepoints"].mean()
    median_count = temporal_counts["num_timepoints"].median()
    max_count = temporal_counts["num_timepoints"].max()
    min_count = temporal_counts["num_timepoints"].min()

    print(f"Mean number of unique timepoints: {mean_count:.2f}")
    print(f"Median number of unique timepoints: {median_count:.2f}")
    print(f"Max number of unique timepoints: {max_count:.2f}")
    print(f"Min number of unique timepoints: {min_count:.2f}")

    # Assign each coordinate pair its sorted index
    temporal_counts["pair_index"] = temporal_counts.index

    ######## OUTLIER ANALYSIS ########

    # Merge sorted indices into the filtered data
    groundwater_plot = groundwater_filtered.merge(
        temporal_counts[
            ["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude", "pair_index"]
        ],
        on=["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude"],
        how="left"
    )

    # Calculate nitrate statistics for each coordinate pair
    result_stats = (
        groundwater_plot.groupby("pair_index")["nitrate_mg_L"]
        .agg(["median", "max", "min", "mean", "std"])
    )

    # Difference between maximum and minimum
    result_stats["max_minus_min"] = (
        result_stats["max"] - result_stats["min"]
    )

    threshold = 10

    # Identify coordinate pairs exceeding the variability threshold OVERALL
    high_variability = result_stats[
        result_stats["max_minus_min"] > threshold
    ]

    # Get coordinate pairs exceeding the threshold
    high_variability_locations = temporal_counts.loc[
        temporal_counts["pair_index"].isin(high_variability.index),
        ["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude"]
    ].drop_duplicates()

    # Retrieve all original groundwater columns for those locations
    selected_groundwater = groundwater.merge(
        high_variability_locations,
        on=["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude"],
        how="inner"
    )

    print(
        f"\nAll locations with overall nitrate concentration ranges "
        f"(max-min) exceeding {threshold} mg/L:"
    )

    display(
        selected_groundwater[
            selected_groundwater["gm_samp_collection_date"].dt.year.between(
                start_year, end_year
            )
        ]
    )

    ######## EXCLUDING DATA ########

    # Temporarily add year to the period dataframe to allow year-level grouping
    groundwater_period = groundwater_period.copy()
    groundwater_period["_year"] = groundwater_period["gm_samp_collection_date"].dt.year

    # 1. Condition A: Max-Min > threshold IN THAT SPECIFIC YEAR
    yearly_stats = groundwater_period.groupby(["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude", "_year"]).agg(
        max_nitrate=("nitrate_mg_L", "max"),
        min_nitrate=("nitrate_mg_L", "min")
    ).reset_index()
    yearly_stats["max_minus_min"] = yearly_stats["max_nitrate"] - yearly_stats["min_nitrate"]

    # 2. Condition B: Location has multiple well IDs overall
    overall_wells = groundwater_period.groupby(["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude"]).agg(
        unique_wells=("gm_well_id", "nunique")
    ).reset_index()

    # Combine both conditions
    exclusion_stats = yearly_stats.merge(overall_wells, on=["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude"])

    # Identify the exact (lat, lon, year) groups to drop
    locations_years_to_exclude = exclusion_stats[
        (exclusion_stats["max_minus_min"] > threshold) & 
        (exclusion_stats["unique_wells"] > 1)
    ][["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude", "_year"]]

    # Filter groundwater_period to exclude those groups
    groundwater_period = groundwater_period.merge(
        locations_years_to_exclude.assign(exclude=True),
        on=["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude", "_year"],
        how="left"
    )

    groundwater_period = (
        groundwater_period[groundwater_period["exclude"].isna()]
        .drop(columns=["exclude", "_year"])
        .copy()
    )

    print(f"\nLocation-years excluded: {len(locations_years_to_exclude)}")
    print(f"Remaining measurements: {len(groundwater_period)}")

    ######## PLOTTING ########

    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
    plt.plot(
        temporal_counts.index,
        temporal_counts["num_timepoints"],
        "."
    )
    plt.xlabel("Latitude-Longitude Pair Index (sorted)")
    plt.ylabel("Number of Unique Time Datapoints")
    plt.title(
        f"[{start_year}-{end_year}] Temporal Coverage Across Locations"
    )
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()

    # Sort by increasing difference between maximum and minimum
    result_stats = result_stats.sort_values(
        "max_minus_min"
    ).reset_index(drop=True)

    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
    plt.plot(
        result_stats.index,
        result_stats["max_minus_min"],
        ".",
        markersize=3
    )
    plt.xlabel("Latitude-Longitude Pair Index")
    plt.ylabel("Maximum Result − Minimum Result")
    plt.title(
        f"[{start_year}-{end_year}] Difference Between Maximum "
        "and Minimum Result by Location"
    )
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()

    return groundwater_period

title: Feature Selection

0. Setup
Objective: Load the integrated lag-1 dataset and confirm its dimensions before screening features. Each row is one nitrate sample; repeated wells are handled later through the team’s 10 km spatial folds rather than by averaging.

title: Feature Selection
text:
1. Feature Inventory
Objective: Classify all 147 columns into the target, candidate predictor groups (soils, terrain, climate, land use), quality-control/coverage columns, and metadata. This inventory is the starting point for every selection decision that follows.


Code
TARGET = "nitrate_mg_L"

METADATA = [
    "gm_well_id", "gm_well_category", "gm_samp_collection_date", "gm_latitude", "gm_longitude",
    "year", "source_csv_row", "observation_id", "crop_year", "measurement_year",
    "dwr_map_status", "change_base_year", "crop_source_match",
]
TERRAIN = ["elevation_m", "topographic_position"]
CLIMATE_KEYWORDS = ("precip", "temperature")


def feature_group(col):
    """Assign each column to one group based on its name."""
    if col == TARGET:
        return "target"
    if col in METADATA:
        return "metadata"
    if (col.endswith("coverage_pct") or "status" in col or "buffer_area" in col
            or "dwr_polygon_area" in col or "dwr_polygon_footprint_pct" in col):
        return "qc_coverage"
    if col.startswith("soil_"):
        return "soils"
    if col in TERRAIN:
        return "terrain"
    if any(k in col for k in CLIMATE_KEYWORDS):
        return "climate"
    if col.startswith("delta_"):
        return "land_use_delta"
    if col.endswith("__previous"):
        return "land_use_previous"
    return "land_use_current"


inventory = pd.DataFrame({"feature": df.columns})
inventory["group"] = inventory["feature"].map(feature_group)

inventory["group"].value_counts()

title: Feature Selection
text:
2. Domain and Metadata Exclusion
Objective: Remove columns that are not environmental predictors (identifiers, dates, bookkeeping, raw coordinates, and data-quality/coverage columns) and the t-2 land-use columns, which are fully redundant with current land use plus annual change. Well category (domestic vs. irrigation/industrial) is retained as a candidate. Every decision is logged as feature, step, decision, reason.


Code
decisions = []


def log_decision(features, step, decision, reason):
    """Record one selection decision per feature."""
    for f in features:
        decisions.append({"feature": f, "step": step, "decision": decision, "reason": reason})


by_group = inventory.groupby("group")["feature"].apply(list)

COORDINATES = ["gm_latitude", "gm_longitude"]
WELL_ATTRIBUTES = ["gm_well_category"]  # kept as a candidate predictor
other_metadata = [f for f in METADATA if f not in COORDINATES + WELL_ATTRIBUTES]

log_decision(other_metadata, "domain", "drop",
             "identifier, date or bookkeeping column; not an environmental predictor")
log_decision(COORDINATES, "domain", "drop",
             "raw coordinates; location alone showed no skill under 10 km spatial folds, "
             "and coordinates can let the model memorize areas instead of learning from land conditions")
log_decision(by_group["qc_coverage"], "domain", "drop",
             "data-quality or coverage column; documents processing, not land conditions")
log_decision(by_group["land_use_previous"], "redundancy", "drop",
             "t-2 land use; equals current minus delta exactly, so current + delta keep the same information")

log = pd.DataFrame(decisions)
candidates = [f for f in df.columns if f not in set(log["feature"]) and f != TARGET]

print(log.groupby(["step", "decision"]).size())
print(f"\nCandidates remaining: {len(candidates)}")

title: Feature Selection
text:
3. Soil Class Consolidation
Objective: Combine sparse soil classes into meaningful groups before screening for low information. Seven drainage classes are grouped by drainage speed (rapid, moderate, slow), and the dual hydrologic group C/D is merged into D, following the USDA convention that C/D soils behave as D when undrained.
Grouping preserves the signal of rare classes (e.g., very poorly drained soils, present at only 7 wells) instead of discarding them.


Code
DRAINAGE_GROUPS = {
    "soil_drainage_rapid_pct": ["excessively_drained", "somewhat_excessively_drained"],
    "soil_drainage_moderate_pct": ["well_drained", "moderately_well_drained"],
    "soil_drainage_slow_pct": ["somewhat_poorly_drained", "poorly_drained", "very_poorly_drained"],
}
HYDGROUP_D = ["soil_hydgrpdcd_pct_c_d", "soil_hydgrpdcd_pct_d"]

new_cols = {}

for new_col, classes in DRAINAGE_GROUPS.items():
    original = [f"soil_drclassdcd_pct_{c}" for c in classes]
    new_cols[new_col] = df[original].sum(axis=1, min_count=1)
    log_decision(original, "domain", "combine", f"merged into {new_col} (grouped by drainage speed)")
    candidates = [f for f in candidates if f not in original] + [new_col]

new_cols["soil_hydgrp_d_pct"] = df[HYDGROUP_D].sum(axis=1, min_count=1)
log_decision(HYDGROUP_D, "domain", "combine",
             "merged into soil_hydgrp_d_pct; C/D soils behave as D when undrained (USDA convention)")
candidates = [f for f in candidates if f not in HYDGROUP_D] + ["soil_hydgrp_d_pct"]

df = pd.concat([df, pd.DataFrame(new_cols)], axis=1)

# Check: the grouped classes should still add up to 100% of the mapped soil area
drainage_total = df[list(DRAINAGE_GROUPS)].sum(axis=1)
hydgroup_total = df[["soil_hydgrpdcd_pct_a", "soil_hydgrpdcd_pct_b",
                     "soil_hydgrpdcd_pct_c", "soil_hydgrp_d_pct"]].sum(axis=1, min_count=1)

print(f"Drainage groups sum to: {drainage_total.min():.1f} - {drainage_total.max():.1f}")
print(f"Hydrologic groups sum to: {hydgroup_total.min():.1f} - {hydgroup_total.max():.1f}")
print(f"Candidates remaining: {len(candidates)}")

text:
4. Low Information
Objective: Remove candidates with more than 50% missing values or with a single value in more than 95% of rows. This screen does not use nitrate, so it can be applied to the full dataset without leakage.


Code
MISSING_THRESHOLD = 0.50
DOMINANT_THRESHOLD = 0.95

missing_share = df[candidates].isna().mean()
dominant_share = df[candidates].apply(lambda s: s.value_counts(normalize=True).iloc[0])

too_missing = missing_share[missing_share > MISSING_THRESHOLD].index.tolist()
near_constant = dominant_share[dominant_share > DOMINANT_THRESHOLD].index.tolist()

log_decision(too_missing, "low_information", "drop",
             f"more than {MISSING_THRESHOLD:.0%} missing values")
log_decision(near_constant, "low_information", "drop",
             f"one value in more than {DOMINANT_THRESHOLD:.0%} of rows")

candidates = [f for f in candidates if f not in too_missing + near_constant]

print("Too many missing:", {f: round(missing_share[f], 2) for f in too_missing})
print("Near-constant:", {f: round(dominant_share[f], 3) for f in near_constant})
print(f"Candidates remaining: {len(candidates)}")

title: Feature Selection
text:
5. Redundancy
Objective: Remove duplicated information without using nitrate. (1) Land-use shares are expressed as a percentage of the whole buffer (pct), so the _of_mapped versions are dropped; the unmapped share is kept through outside_dwr_polygons_pct. (2) When the same variable at 500 m and 1,000 m has Spearman ρ > 0.9, only the 500 m version is kept, matching the soil buffer scale and the area closest to the well. Correlations across different variables (e.g., crop intensity vs. elevation) are not used to drop features; their added value is assessed in the model-based step.


Code
RADIUS_THRESHOLD = 0.90

# 1. Keep pct (share of whole buffer); drop the share-of-mapped-area versions
of_mapped = [f for f in candidates if "_of_mapped_" in f]
log_decision(of_mapped, "redundancy", "drop",
             "share of DWR-mapped area; pct (share of whole buffer) is used instead, "
             "with outside_dwr_polygons_pct describing the unmapped share")
candidates = [f for f in candidates if f not in of_mapped]

# 2. Compare each variable at 500 m vs 1,000 m
pairs = [(f, f.replace("500m", "1000m")) for f in candidates
         if "500m" in f and f.replace("500m", "1000m") in candidates]

radius = pd.DataFrame(
    [{"feature_500m": a, "feature_1000m": b,
      "spearman": df[[a, b]].corr(method="spearman").iloc[0, 1]} for a, b in pairs]
).sort_values("spearman", ascending=False)

redundant_1000m = radius.loc[radius["spearman"] > RADIUS_THRESHOLD, "feature_1000m"].tolist()
log_decision(redundant_1000m, "redundancy", "drop",
             f"Spearman rho > {RADIUS_THRESHOLD} with the 500 m version; 500 m kept")
candidates = [f for f in candidates if f not in redundant_1000m]

display(radius.round(2))
print(f"Candidates remaining: {len(candidates)}")

title: Feature Selection
text:
7. Conclusions
Summary. The integrated dataset (5,280 nitrate samples, 1,993 wells, 147 columns) was screened to 50 candidate features for modeling through four model-independent steps: domain and metadata exclusion (147 → 76), soil class consolidation (→ 71), low-information screening (→ 69), and redundancy removal (→ 50). No step used nitrate values, so the screening carries no target leakage. All decisions are logged in results/feature_selection.csv.
Key decisions and rationale - Unit of analysis: each nitrate sample is one row. Samples are not averaged per well because crop (lag-1) and antecedent climate features change from year to year; averaging would remove the temporal information these features carry. Repeated and nearby wells will be handled through the team’s 10 km spatial folds. - Coordinates excluded: a location-only model showed no skill under 10 km spatial folds, and raw coordinates could let the model memorize areas instead of learning from land conditions. - Well category retained: domestic vs. irrigation/industrial wells may differ in depth, but well depth is not available to confirm this. - t−2 land use removed: current land use minus the t−2 value equals the annual change exactly, so current land use plus annual change keep all the information. - Soil classes consolidated: seven drainage classes were grouped by drainage speed (rapid, moderate, slow), and hydrologic group C/D was merged into D (USDA convention), preserving the signal of rare classes such as very poorly drained soils (7 wells). - Low information: depth to bedrock (73% missing) and 500 m urban change (zero in 96% of rows, possibly a mapping artifact) were removed. - Land-use definition: shares are expressed as a percentage of the whole buffer (pct), with outside_dwr_polygons_pct describing the unmapped share. When the 500 m and 1,000 m versions of a variable had Spearman ρ > 0.9, the 500 m version was kept. - Correlations across variable types were not used to drop features. Agricultural intensity, elevation, slope, and precipitation overlap strongly (see EDA), and which of them adds predictive value should be decided by model evaluation, not by pairwise correlation.
Next steps for modeling - Train tree-based models (e.g., decision tree, random forest) on the 50 candidates using the 10 km spatial folds and the space-time split. - Assess feature contributions with grouped permutation importance (soils, terrain, climate, agricultural intensity, land-use change) to account for correlated predictors. - Compare the full 50-feature set with reduced sets by cross-validated RMSE.
Caveats - Drainage groups and hydrologic groups each sum to 100%, so one group in each set is redundant by construction; this matters for linear models but not for tree-based models. - Spearman correlations in the results table use the full dataset and are descriptive only; they were not used for selection. - The 2024 DWR crop map is provisional and feeds the 2025 test year of the space-time evaluation. The one-year crop lag is a modeling assumption, not an established nitrate transport time.
Update after modeling: subbasin indicators (one 0/1 column per groundwater subbasin) were later added as an optional feature group through load_model_data(subbasin=True) (add_subbasin and subbasin_dummies in src/features/transformers.py, using data/salinas_valley_subbasins.geojson), which by default also drops elevation. Model notebooks report results with and without subbasin.

title: Final Results: Hold-Out Evaluation
text:
Objective: Evaluate the selected models once on the hold-out fold (fold 4), which no model, tuning step or threshold choice has used. These are the numbers to report as final performance.
Selected models (best mean over folds 0–3 in classification_models.ipynb and regression_models.ipynb, configuration 10km_subbasin with subbasin features): - Classification (exceeds 10 mg/L): random forest (AUC 0.827, Brier skill 0.291), with the dummy baseline for reference. - Regression (log nitrate): random forest (RMSE 0.973, R² 0.343), with the dummy baseline for reference.
Procedure 1. Each final model is tuned and fit on all development data (folds 0–3), with exactly the same settings and search as in the model notebooks. 2. The classification threshold is fixed before looking at the hold-out: by default, the threshold with the best F1 on the out-of-fold predictions of folds 0–3. 3. Each model predicts fold 4 once; scores are compared with the cross-validation results.
Rule: run the final evaluation only once, after the team agrees on the models and the threshold. Keep RUN_FINAL_EVALUATION = False until then: the notebook performs a dry run that treats fold 3 as a stand-in test set (training on folds 0–2), so the code can be checked without touching fold 4.

title: Final Results: Hold-Out Evaluation
text:
2. Classification threshold
Fixed by the team before the evaluation at 0.4: the thresholds that maximize F1 on the out-of-fold predictions of folds 0–3 are 0.35–0.37 for the random forest. A threshold below 0.5 catches more exceeding wells (higher recall) at the cost of more false alarms, which suits drinking-water screening, where missing a contaminated well is worse than an extra sample.


Code
if THRESHOLD is None:
    oof = pd.read_csv(predictions_path("classification", SPLIT, USE_SUBBASIN))
    candidates = np.round(np.arange(0.05, 0.951, 0.01), 2)
    f1 = [f1_score(oof["exceeds"], (oof["Random forest"] >= t).astype(int)) for t in candidates]
    THRESHOLD = float(candidates[int(np.argmax(f1))])
    print(f"Threshold chosen on folds 0-3 out-of-fold predictions: {THRESHOLD:.2f} (F1 = {max(f1):.3f})")
else:
    print(f"Threshold set by hand: {THRESHOLD:.2f}")

title: Final Results: Hold-Out Evaluation
text:
5c. Feature importance
How much the final random forest classifier relies on each feature: each feature is shuffled in the test fold and the drop in AUC is measured (permutation importance, 20 repeats). The subbasin indicator columns are shuffled together as one feature.


Code
from joblib import Parallel, delayed

# Permutation importance: shuffle one feature (or one group of features) in the test fold and measure how much the hold-out AUC drops. A large drop means the model relies on that feature. The subbasin indicator columns are shuffled together, as one feature, since they describe one variable.
N_REPEATS = 20

rf = final_models["Random forest classifier"]
subbasin_cols = [f for f in FEATURES if f.startswith("subbasin_")]
groups = {f: [f] for f in FEATURES if f not in subbasin_cols}
if subbasin_cols:
    groups["subbasin"] = subbasin_cols

X_test, y_test = test[FEATURES], test["exceeds"]
base_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, rf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])


def auc_drops(cols, seed):
    """Drop in AUC for each of N_REPEATS shuffles of these columns (shuffled together)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    drops = []
    for _ in range(N_REPEATS):
        shuffled = X_test.copy()
        shuffled[cols] = shuffled[cols].to_numpy()[rng.permutation(len(shuffled))]
        drops.append(base_auc - roc_auc_score(y_test, rf.predict_proba(shuffled)[:, 1]))
    return drops


# One feature per CPU core; each feature has its own seed, so the result does not depend on the number of cores
results = Parallel(n_jobs=-1)(delayed(auc_drops)(cols, seed) for seed, cols in enumerate(groups.values()))

# Impurity importance (how much each feature's splits reduce impurity in training), for comparison;
# it tends to favour continuous features, so the permutation result is the one to report
impurity = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=FEATURES)
if subbasin_cols:
    impurity["subbasin"] = impurity[subbasin_cols].sum()

importance = (pd.DataFrame({
    "feature": list(groups),
    "auc_drop_mean": [np.mean(d) for d in results],
    "auc_drop_std": [np.std(d) for d in results]
}).assign(impurity_importance=lambda d: d["feature"].map(impurity))
.sort_values("auc_drop_mean", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True))
print(f"Hold-out AUC with no shuffling: {base_auc:.3f}")
display(importance.head(15).round(4))

INTERPRETABILITY = paths.FIGURES["interpretability"]
INTERPRETABILITY.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
importance.to_csv(INTERPRETABILITY / f"permutation_importance_classifier_{TAG}.csv", index=False)

top = importance.head(15).iloc[::-1]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
ax.barh(top["feature"], top["auc_drop_mean"], xerr=top["auc_drop_std"], color="#2a78d6")
ax.axvline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(INTERPRETABILITY / f"permutation_importance_classifier_{TAG}.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

title: Final Results: Hold-Out Evaluation
text:
6. Conclusions

Classification (random forest): hold-out AUC = 0.741 (cross-validation 0.827, range 0.796–0.871 across folds), Brier skill = 0.209 (0.291). At the agreed threshold of 0.4, the model detects 74% of samples exceeding 10 mg/L (recall), and 59% of the samples it flags actually exceed the limit (precision); F1 = 0.654.
Regression (random forest): hold-out RMSE (log) = 1.053 vs. 1.237 for the dummy baseline, a 15% reduction (19% in cross-validation); R² = 0.170 (cross-validation 0.343).
Generalization: hold-out performance is lower than in cross-validation. The hold-out fold is a harder area: it contains about half of the East Side Aquifer samples, the most contaminated subbasin, and 42% of its samples exceed 10 mg/L versus 32% in the development data. The dummy regressor’s negative R² (−0.15) on the hold-out reflects this shift in nitrate levels. Relative to the baseline, the random forest still improves predictions by a similar margin as in cross-validation.
Caveats: a single hold-out fold covers a limited set of areas, so its score is more uncertain than the four-fold cross-validation mean; both should be reported. Performance applies to the Salinas Valley; transfer to other basins was not tested.

The fitted final models are saved in data/models/ (local) for the risk map notebook.

title: Groundwater Nitrate — Integrated Dataset EDA (Historical Lag-1)
text:
5. Historical Agricultural Features — Lag-1 EDA
Objective: Review the already-computed availability and Spearman correlations of agricultural predictors from the year before each nitrate observation.
Temporal assumption: Year t nitrate is joined to year t−1 crop features to represent preceding agricultural conditions and avoid using later-in-year land use; this is not evidence that nitrate travels through the aquifer in one year. Maps published after a sampling date also mean these results are retrospective, not necessarily deployable at that past date. Consider alternative lag periods only in future analysis.
Coverage caveat: A successfully matched crop record or non-missing variable is not proof of complete mapped land cover within a buffer. The DWR polygon footprint represents mapped polygons, not the entire landscape.

6. Feature Relationships & Redundancy
Objective: Review the previously computed seven-feature Spearman heatmap, focusing on how agricultural intensity relates to other agriculture variables, slope, elevation, and historical precipitation.
Scope: Seven intentionally selected example features, not all 147 columns. Identifiers, target values, coverage metadata and other variables are excluded from this display, and no feature is removed based on correlation alone.


Code

# Compare agricultural and environmental predictors.
# Use one median value per well-year to avoid overweighting repeated samples.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

feature_labels = {
    "crop_cycles_500m": "Crop cycles",
    "pct_multicrop_1000m": "Multicrop",
    "pct_veg_berry_500m": "Vegetables & berries",
    "pct_cropland_500m": "Cropland",
    "soil_slopegradwta": "Soil slope",
    "elevation_m": "Elevation",
    "historical_mean_annual_precip_mm": "Historical precipitation"
}

well_year_features = (
    df.groupby(["gm_well_id", "year"])[list(feature_labels)]
    .median()
)

# Calculate Spearman correlations between predictors.
feature_corr = well_year_features.corr(method="spearman")
plot_corr = feature_corr.rename(
    index=feature_labels,
    columns=feature_labels
)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))

sns.heatmap(
    plot_corr,
    annot=True,
    fmt=".2f",
    cmap="RdBu_r",
    center=0,
    vmin=-1,
    vmax=1,
    square=True
)

plt.title("Agricultural and Environmental Feature Correlations")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Key Findings — Agricultural and Environmental Redundancy (saved heatmap)

Crop cycles and multicrop area: ρ = +0.90.
Multicrop and vegetables/berries: ρ = +0.93.
Agricultural predictors are negatively correlated with soil slope (e.g., multicrop vs. slope ρ = −0.78) and elevation (multicrop vs. elevation ρ = −0.79).
Soil slope and elevation: ρ = +0.72.

These values are associations among predictors, not direct effects on nitrate. Their geographic structure could explain part of the agricultural–nitrate associations. Collinearity and contributions to predictive performance still require group-aware model validation; no variables are excluded here.

title: Regression models
text:
Code
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2


Here, we run all our regression models so that we can compare them side-by-side. We compare a dummy model and simple linear model to linear models with two regularization strategies (ridge and lasso), a decision tree model, a random forest model, and a boosted regression tree model. Hyperparameters are tuned with GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV in each set of training folds, holding one whole fold out at the time, so the test fold is never used for tuning. We also run our models on several different splits to understand the limits of our models.


Code

The following cell is used to set up necessary variables and define the parameter grids used for hyperparameter tuning.


Code
RMSE = "neg_root_mean_squared_error"    # Scoring method
TREE_DEPTHS = [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 15]    # For the decision tree model 
RF_GRID = {
    "max_depth": [6, 8, 11, 15, None], 
    "max_features": ["sqrt", 0.3, 0.5], 
    "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 20]
}   # For the random forest model
BRT_GRID = {
    "learning_rate": [0.03, 0.05], 
    "n_estimators": [20, 35, 50, 75, 100], 
    "max_depth": [2, 3, 4], 
    "min_child_weight": [5, 20, 50], 
    "subsample": [0.5, 0.7]
} # For the boosted regression tree model




Code
def linear_pipe(model):
    """Impute and standardize inside each training fold, then fit the linear model."""
    return make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler(), model)


The following cell contains our list of regression models.


Code
REGRESSION_MODELS = {
    "Dummy (mean)": ("Team", lambda: DummyRegressor(strategy="mean"), all_features),
    "Linear regression": ("Andrea", lambda: linear_pipe(LinearRegression()), linear_features),
    "Ridge": ("Andrea", lambda: tuned(linear_pipe(Ridge()), {"ridge__alpha": np.logspace(0, 6, 13)}, RMSE), linear_features),
    "Lasso": ("Andrea", lambda: tuned(linear_pipe(Lasso(max_iter=20_000)), {"lasso__alpha": [0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5]}, RMSE), linear_features),
    "Decision tree": ("Gavin", lambda: tuned(DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_leaf=20, random_state=0), {"max_depth": TREE_DEPTHS}, RMSE), all_features),
    "Random forest": ("Charlsey", lambda: tuned(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=1), RF_GRID, RMSE, n_iter=10), all_features),
    "XGBoost BRT": ("Karuna", lambda: tuned(xgboost.XGBRegressor(objective="reg:squarederror", max_bin=64, random_state=0, n_jobs=1), BRT_GRID, RMSE, n_iter=20), all_features),
}

def panels(n, ncols=3, width=4.5, height=3.8):
    """A grid with one panel per model; unused panels are hidden."""
    nrows = -(-n // ncols)
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width * ncols, height * nrows), squeeze=False)
    axs = axs.ravel()
    for ax in axs[n:]:
        ax.set_axis_off()
    return fig, axs


def save(fig, name):
    fig.savefig(FIGURES / f"{name}_{CONFIG[0]}_subbasin{int(CONFIG[1])}.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
